payload.title: What Are the Greek Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.excerpt: Greek wedding traditions in the order a couple meets them: the koumbaros, stefana and common cup, krevati, koufeta and the dances, plus what Australians need to marry legally in Greece.
payload.author: Wedded Wonderland
key_takeaways: The Orthodox wedding service has no vows, and the crowning of the couple, not a kiss, is the moment most guests watch for.
Customs such as the krevati, names on the shoe and koufeta are family folklore that varies by region, so ask your own family how they do it.
At the reception, the kalamatianos, the money dance and a chorus of "na zisete" often matter more to families than any formal programme.
To marry legally in Greece, check with the Greek municipality and the Australian Embassy in Athens about a Certificate of No Impediment, an apostille and any fees, as at November 2026.

faq.q: What are the most common Greek wedding traditions?
faq.a: Inside the church, the crowning with stefana, the common cup and the Dance of Isaiah. Around it, the krevati, names on the bride's shoe, koufeta for guests, and circle dances such as the kalamatianos at the reception.

faq.q: Why do Greeks pretend to spit at weddings?
faq.a: The light "ftou ftou" sound is often told as a way of warding off the evil eye after praising someone. It is a folk custom, not a church one, and no one actually spits.

faq.q: What do the stefana crowns mean?
faq.a: The Church explains them as crowns of God's glory, crowning the couple as His children and witnesses in this world and heirs of His Kingdom. The ribbon that joins them is usually described as a sign of the two lives joined.

faq.q: Why are koufeta given in odd numbers?
faq.a: The reason often told is that an odd number cannot be divided, like the couple.

faq.q: Why does the bride step on the groom's foot?
faq.a: It is folklore. As the story goes, whoever steps first has the last word in the marriage.

faq.q: What should I wear to a Greek wedding as a guest?
faq.a: Dress modestly for the church, with shoulders covered, as Smartraveller advises for churches in Greece. Then dress for a long party with plenty of dancing.

faq.q: What do you say to the couple at a Greek wedding?
faq.a: "Na zisete", a wish for a long life together.

faq.q: What is a good gift for a Greek wedding?
faq.a: Many families give money in a card, and others use a registry. Ask someone close to the couple what is usual in their family.

images.shot_brief: Real Greek or Greek-Australian Orthodox wedding: couple wearing stefana joined by a ribbon, soft natural or candle light, faces soft or three-quarter, no identifiable children, no venue signage or vendor branding. Landscape 16:9 with room for a title overlay. Couple consent on file.

Close detail: the koumbaros's hands exchanging the rings or crossing the stefana over the couple's heads during the service; or an engagement ring detail on the right hand. Hands and rings in focus, faces out of frame or soft. Church interior light, no clergy faces needed. Consent on file.

Detail of the stefana (two crowns joined by a ribbon) on a tray beside the Gospel or held above the couple, with the tall wedding candles in soft focus. Real ceremony or a real pair of stefana photographed in a parish (with permission). No AI.

Couple, crowned, being led by the priest around the ceremony table (Dance of Isaiah), motion slightly blurred; or the common cup held over the table. Church interior, warm light, faces of guests not identifiable. Consent from couple; parish photography rules respected.

Still life: white sugared almonds (koufeta) in an odd number, tied in tulle or in a small dish, linen and soft daylight, shallow depth of field. No people, no hands, no cultural dress, no place, no logos. Preferred: licensed photo or a styled in-house shoot. Fallback: AI neutral still life labelled 'Illustrative image' and used only after Nic approves.

Evening reception: guests linked in a circle dance, the leader holding a handkerchief, warm light, motion blur welcome, faces soft or turned, no identifiable children, no money pinned or plates (avoid cost cues). Consent from couple and no identifiable guests without release.

Greek landscape that reads as a wedding destination without naming a venue: whitewashed island chapel or Aegean coastline at golden hour, no people, no venue signage, no identifiable private property. Licensed stock or library; location verified by register or EXIF and named only at town or island level in the caption.
